notes: Summary judgment on consortium tax relief repayment claim; contract and restitution arguments clearly rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Consortium tax relief repayment after subsidiary share sale
key_facts: Interservefm and AMEC formed a joint venture through HMC for a Cumbria hospital; tax losses were surrendered to group subsidiaries including Omnisure.
Omnisure, then a wholly owned subsidiary of Interservefm, used consortium relief to save £368,164 in tax.
Interservefm sold Omnisure's shares to SGI under a SPA in August 1999; inter-company debts were settled but the £368,000 consortium relief item was excluded from the net payment.
Interservefm claimed an implied contract or restitutionary repayment of the tax benefit, relying on audited and completion accounts showing a consortium relief creditor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for summary judgment and strike out, with the claimant seeking permission to amend the claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to amend refused and summary judgment entered for the defendant; the amended contract and restitution claims had no real prospect of success.
enrichment.ratio: An agreement to repay consortium tax relief cannot be implied from conduct where the group as a whole benefited from the losses at surrender, the accounts distinguished consortium relief from debts owed to the parent, and no payment was demanded before or at the share sale; a restitution claim fails because there was no unjust enrichment where the group received the intended tax benefit.
legal_issues: Whether an implied contract arose from surrender and use of tax losses
Whether audited accounts evidenced a debt due to the claimant
Whether tax losses were transferred under a mistake of fact
Whether the proposed amended claim should be permitted

confidence.notes: Outcome and reasoning on implied contract and restitution are explicit throughout the judgment.

notes: Vexatious litigant civil proceedings order under section 42; extensive litigation history and order terms are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Civil proceedings order against habitual vexatious litigant
key_facts: The Attorney General applied under section 42 of the Supreme Court Act 1981 for a civil proceedings order against Mrs Fradkina.
Since 1998 Mrs Fradkina had instituted about 30 separate claims and been involved in 34 appeals, largely concerning housing and care of her son.
She repeatedly re-litigated struck-out claims, breached a section 91(14) Children Act order, and failed to comply with multiple costs orders.
An extended civil restraint order had previously failed to deter further litigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by the Attorney General for a civil proceedings order on the ground of habitual vexatious litigation.
enrichment.outcome: Civil proceedings order made prohibiting Mrs Fradkina from instituting or continuing civil proceedings or making applications without leave of the High Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where a person habitually and persistently institutes vexatious civil proceedings and applications without reasonable ground, the High Court may and in an appropriate case should make a civil proceedings order under section 42 to protect the administration of justice.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Fradkina had habitually and persistently instituted vexatious proceedings
Whether those proceedings were without reasonable ground
Whether a civil proceedings order was appropriate

confidence.notes: Statutory test, factual history, and order terms are set out directly in the judgment.

notes: Detailed trade mark infringement and validity judgment on COMPASS marks; LTJ Diffusion and Article 8(4) CTM analysis is thorough.

enrichment.short_title: COMPASS trade mark infringement and partial invalidity

statutes_considered.title: Council Regulation (EC) No 40/94 on the Community trade mark

key_facts: Compass Publishing BV owned UK and Community COMPASS marks for business and IT consultancy; Compass Logistics Ltd traded under Compass Logistics in logistics consultancy.
The defendant used COMPASS alone and COMPASS LOGISTICS; there was no evidence of marketplace confusion over eight years.
The claimant succeeded on infringement of the CTM and 1988 UK mark but the 1996 UK mark was partially invalid for logistics consultancy.
The defendant's prior goodwill in COMPASS LOGISTICS was too small and of mere local significance to invalidate the CTM under Article 8(4).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial on trade mark infringement claims and Part 20 revocation and invalidity counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded on infringement; defendant's validity challenge failed save that the 1996 UK mark was invalid to the extent covering logistics consultancy in the United Kingdom.
enrichment.ratio: COMPASS LOGISTICS is not identical to COMPASS under Article 9.1(a)/LTJ Diffusion but likelihood of confusion exists under Article 9.1(b); a trader with passing-off rights may invoke Article 8(4) but prior unregistered rights of mere local significance do not invalidate a CTM; honest concurrent use cannot assist against Community rights.
legal_issues: Whether COMPASS LOGISTICS is identical or confusingly similar to COMPASS
Whether the defendant's prior use could invalidate the CTM under Article 8(4)
Whether the 1988 UK mark covered the defendant's services and had been used
Whether the 1996 UK mark was invalid for logistics consultancy by passing off
linked_authorities: LTJ Diffusion SA v Sadas Vertbaudet SA (Case C-291/00) [2003] ETMR 83
Reed Executive plc v Reed Business Information Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 159
Decon Laboratories v Fred Baker Scientific [2001] RPC 293
Sabel BV v Puma AG [1998] RPC 199

confidence.notes: Infringement and validity conclusions are detailed and explicit; equitable relief scope was expressly reserved.

notes: Family committal appeal for non-molestation breach; sentence reduction and Hale v Tanner guidance clearly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Committal sentence reduced for injunction breach by driving past home
key_facts: Mr Aquilina breached a renewed non-molestation injunction restraining him from coming within 200 metres of his wife and children's address.
He had previously been sentenced to 56 days' imprisonment for earlier breaches and was released before driving past the home at night on 11 November 2003.
Judge Masterman sentenced him to six months' imprisonment for the third breach; the breach involved no violence, stopping, or gesticulating.
The appeal concerned the severity of the committal sentence rather than liability for contempt.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a six-month committal sentence for breach of a family injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; six-month sentence quashed and replaced with three months' imprisonment, with immediate release.
enrichment.ratio: Committal for breach of a family injunction should balance coercion and punishment with securing future compliance; where the breach was comparatively minor and non-violent, a six-month sentence giving undue weight to punishing contumacy was manifestly excessive.
legal_issues: Appropriate sentence for breach of a non-molestation injunction
Balance between punitive and coercive purposes of committal
Whether the judge erred in sentencing for contempt rather than future compliance

confidence.notes: Facts of the breach, prior history, and sentencing reasoning are clearly stated, though detailed background violence is not fully explored.

notes: Case stated on blood specimen refusal and PACE legal advice; domestic authority and Article 6 delay analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Blood specimen refusal: no delay for legal advice under PACE
key_facts: Mr Myles failed a roadside breath test; mouth alcohol rendered the station breathalyser unreliable and he refused a required blood specimen at the police station.
He had declined a solicitor earlier but later said he required further legal advice when blood was requested.
The Crown Court dismissed his appeal, holding domestic law did not require delay for legal advice before specimen procedures.
The case stated appeal was delayed by over eighteen months through no fault of the appellant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from the Crown Court after conviction for failing to provide a blood specimen.
enrichment.outcome: Both case stated questions answered affirmatively on the specimen issue; appeal allowed only to quash the financial penalty because of Article 6 delay, leaving conviction, disqualification, and costs orders intact.
enrichment.ratio: Under domestic road traffic and PACE authorities, obtaining breath or blood specimens must not be delayed to any significant extent for general legal advice where a suspect has already declined a solicitor; Article 6 breach by procedural delay may justify reducing financial penalties but cannot override mandatory disqualification absent special reasons.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to delay blood sampling for legal advice breached PACE section 58
Whether Article 6(3)(c) required legal advice before specimen procedures
Whether Commonwealth authorities altered domestic law
Whether Article 6 delay could amount to special reasons avoiding disqualification
linked_authorities: R v Wickens [1958] 42 Cr App R 236

confidence.notes: Primary legal conclusions and partial appeal outcome are explicit; certification of a broader special reasons point was refused.

notes: Prosecution reopening after no case submission on plating certificate evidence; discretion principles and affirmative answers are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Prosecution reopening after lacuna on plating certificate
key_facts: Mr Tuck was convicted of exceeding permitted axle weight on a Ford lorry after a dynamic weighbridge check on the A23.
At close of prosecution evidence there was no proof of a plating certificate or permitted axle weight from column 2 of that certificate.
Magistrates allowed the prosecution to reopen and recall the vehicle inspector, who then gave oral evidence about the ministry plate.
The defendant had challenged only the weighbridge accuracy and did not cross-examine on the source of the permitted weight figure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' conviction for exceeding permitted vehicle weight.
enrichment.outcome: All three questions answered in the affirmative; appeal dismissed and conviction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Magistrates have a general discretion to allow the prosecution to reopen its case where a central evidential gap is identified, provided the defendant suffers no real prejudice beyond losing a tactical advantage from the oversight; loss of a windfall acquittal is not sufficient prejudice.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates could reopen the prosecution case after a no case submission
What weight to attach to recalled witness evidence given a ten-month gap and prior omission
Whether the plating certificate and overload were proved to the criminal standard
linked_authorities: R v Pilcher (1974) 60 Cr App R 1
R v Francis (1991) 91 Cr App R 271
R v Munnery [1992] 94 Cr App R 164

confidence.notes: Discretion principles and answers to all three stated questions are directly addressed.

notes: Legal aid statutory charge enforcement appeal; LSC administrative errors and limited interest award on cross-appeal are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid statutory charge: interest and costs after LSC errors
key_facts: The LSC sought to enforce a statutory charge over the Turvills' home for legal aid costs from defending mortgage possession proceedings brought by Michael Kelly.
Taxed costs totalled £15,934.41; the Turvills paid £8,791.73 in September 1999 believing that redeemed the charge in full due to an LSC caseworker error.
Repeated incorrect redemption figures and administrative mistakes led to enforcement proceedings claiming about £7,142.68 plus interest.
The Turvills paid the outstanding principal shortly before trial but denied any further liability for interest or costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against costs order and cross-appeal against refusal of interest on enforcement of a legal aid statutory charge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; cross-appeal allowed in part to award interest of about £90 from service of proceedings until payment; Turvills ordered to pay LSC costs of the action and appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a statutory charge debtor wrongly denies all further liability and forces enforcement proceedings, interest may be awarded from commencement of proceedings despite prior LSC errors, but pre-proceedings interest may be refused where administrative mistakes materially contributed to delay; costs may follow where proceedings were necessary to recover the principal sum.
legal_issues: Whether interest was payable on the outstanding statutory charge balance
Effect of LSC administrative errors on interest and costs discretion
Whether enforcement proceedings were necessary
Whether the judge erred in awarding full action costs after principal payment

confidence.notes: Chronology of LSC errors, principal payment, and appellate re-exercise of interest discretion are thoroughly narrated.

notes: Partial appeal against €4m restitution summary judgment on courier overbilling; head-by-head analysis and leave orders are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Courier overbilling restitution: partial summary judgment appeal
key_facts: Getronics, a computer components supplier, claimed about €4,045,374.75 from its courier Logistic & Transport Consulting for invoices paid without corresponding services.
The claim was pursued in restitution for money had and received after fraud claims failed at summary judgment stage; bogus or duplicate invoicing was alleged.
Master Whittaker gave summary judgment on most heads; the defendant appealed on eight labelled categories of overcharge.
Investigation relied on Amicore files, consignment notes, and WLP computer records; insider witness Ghisdal was treated with caution.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against partial summary judgment on restitution claims following refusal of fraud-based summary relief.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: French and German invoices upheld; excess picking given unconditional leave to defend; inventory management and several stock-movement items given conditional leave to defend on payment in; two-thirds of appeal costs to claimant and one-third costs in the cause.
enrichment.ratio: Summary judgment is appropriate where invoice and consignment evidence shows payments were not due and the defendant offers no credible positive defence or unavailable supporting documents; where subcontractor invoices raise a triable issue on a discrete head, unconditional or conditional leave to defend may be granted even in a large restitution claim.
legal_issues: Whether sample invoice analysis justified summary judgment across all French and German invoices
Whether computer WLP evidence was admissible and sufficient for Italian and inventory claims
Whether Mrs Verdyke's subcontractor evidence created triable issues on excess picking and inventory management
Whether Netherlands shuttle and stock movement payments were recoverable in restitution
linked_authorities: Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England (No 3) [2001] 2 All ER 513
Mulvenna v Royal Bank of Scotland [2003] EWCA Civ 112
S v Gloucester County Council [2000] 3 All ER 346

confidence.notes: Head-by-head outcomes and summary judgment principles are clearly stated; underlying fraud facts were expressly severed from restitution analysis.

notes: Child injured by missile from council demolition site; inadequate trial findings and Smith v Littlewoods remittal clearly ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Child struck by debris from council demolition site
key_facts: Six-year-old Tashan Gabriel was struck in the eye by a stone or mud thrown by children playing on Kirklees Council's Bracken Square demolition site in Huddersfield.
He was walking on the pavement past the unfenced site when injured; excavation work had begun only days earlier.
The council admitted partial excavation and rubble but denied negligence and causation; police had advised against fencing because children might climb it.
The trial judge found no duty of care mainly because there was no evidence of prior missiles being thrown from the site.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from strike-out of negligence claim after trial judge held no duty of care was owed to a passer-by.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to a different judge for retrial on duty, breach, and causation; defendant ordered to pay costs subject to written challenge within 14 days.
enrichment.ratio: Liability for injury caused by third parties on land requires more than bare foreseeability and depends on fact-sensitive findings about sources of danger, knowledge of trespassing children, and abatable risk; a trial judge must make sufficient factual findings on site conditions and council knowledge before concluding no duty exists under Smith v Littlewoods principles.
legal_issues: Whether the council owed a duty of care to a passer-by injured by children on the site
Application of Smith v Littlewoods to third-party wrongdoing
Whether absence of prior incidents negated foreseeability
Whether inadequate findings required remittal
linked_authorities: Jolly v Sutton London Borough Council [2000] 1 WLR 1082
Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Miller Steamship Co Pty [1967] 1 AC 617

confidence.notes: Appellate criticism of inadequate findings and remittal order are explicit; liability on remittal was deliberately not pre-judged.

notes: SCCO assessment of eleven Bridgend housing disrepair CFA cases; unenforceability, legal aid, and proportionality rulings summarised in Appendix 3.

enrichment.short_title: Bridgend housing disrepair CFA costs assessment
key_facts: Eleven consent-order housing disrepair cases against Bridgend CBC were assessed at the SCCO after transfer from Bridgend County Court.
Claimants funded by 100% success fee CFAs and ATE insurance through PD Associates and CMS Investigations under a Fastrack scheme.
Average damages were about £1,631 plus repairs while total costs claimed averaged about £8,012 including success fee, premium, and VAT.
Cases settled before the 2003 housing disrepair pre-action protocol; about 210 similar cases remained pending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment of costs in eleven test housing disrepair cases at the Supreme Court Costs Office.
enrichment.outcome: CFAs held unenforceable for regulatory breaches; ATE premiums disallowed; success fee benchmark 25% if enforceable; base costs over £4,000 disproportionate; Fastrack litigation service fees disallowed; surveyors' reports capped at £250 plus VAT; defendant liability limited essentially to paid disbursements and assessment costs.
enrichment.ratio: Failure materially to comply with CFA Regulations on financing alternatives and related protections can render CFAs unenforceable where litigation was steered into disproportionate and improper cost claims; where legal aid was a reasonable funding choice, ATE premiums are not recoverable; in pre-protocol housing disrepair cases settling before allocation, claimed base costs excluding VAT above about £4,000 are plainly disproportionate.
legal_issues: Enforceability of CFAs under the 2000 Regulations
Whether legal aid availability made CFA/ATE funding unreasonable
Appropriate success fee percentage in late 2001 housing disrepair cases
Proportionality of base costs and recoverability of Fastrack and surveyor fees
linked_authorities: R v Dudley Magistrates Court ex p Power City Stores Ltd (1990) 154 JP 654

confidence.notes: Appendix 3 summarises core rulings clearly; some case-specific CFA signature issues were reserved for further argument.
